dev.question: What is the fundamental mathematical relationship between the width of a signal in time and its width in frequency?

options.A: They are independent of each other.
options.B: Their product is bounded by a constant.
options.C: Their sum is always equal to one.
options.D: One is the derivative of the other.

dev.question: If a pulse in time becomes twice as narrow, what happens to the width of its Fourier transform in frequency?

options.D: It becomes four times as wide.

dev.question: Which function shape minimizes the product of its time width and frequency width?
Why can a signal not be perfectly localized in both time and frequency simultaneously?

What is the Fourier transform of a Dirac delta function δ(t)?
If you increase the duration of a time-domain window by a factor of 4, how does the main lobe width of its spectral leakage change?

options.A: It decreases by a factor of 4.
options.B: It decreases by a factor of 2.
options.C: It increases by a factor of 2.

test.question: Which of the following best illustrates the difference between a sine wave and a square pulse as discussed in the context of waves and signals?

options.A: Both are equally localized in time and frequency.
options.B: A sine wave is periodic and spread out, while a square pulse is localized in time.
options.C: A square pulse is periodic with indefinite frequency, and a sine wave is localized in time.
options.D: Both are highly localized in the frequency domain.

test.question: What does the Fourier Transform allow us to do with a signal?

options.A: Transform a function from one unit system to another.
options.B: Convert a signal between its time/space domain and frequency domain representations.
options.C: Compress a signal to reduce its spread in all domains.
options.D: Eliminate uncertainty in the measurement of signals.

test.question: When discussing the spread or uncertainty of a function, what does a larger variance in the time domain usually mean about its Fourier transform?

options.A: The transformed function will also have a larger variance.
options.B: The spread in the frequency domain decreases as the spread in time increases.
options.C: The variance remains unchanged in both domains.
options.D: The spread in the frequency domain increases as the spread in time increases.

test.question: According to the uncertainty principle shown with the cheetah and whale examples, what happens to the frequency spread as a signal becomes more localized in time?

options.A: It becomes more localized in frequency as well.

test.question: Why is it impossible for a musical instrument to generate a pulse that is perfectly localized in both time and frequency, as shown in the applications section?

options.A: Instruments are limited by mechanical constraints, not physical laws.
options.B: Because to be highly localized in time, the signal must be spread out in frequency, and vice versa, due to the uncertainty principle.
options.C: Because sound cannot be both loud and quiet at the same time.
options.D: It is possible; limitations are only technological.
